# Critical Materials Resilience Strategy
## Specialty Gases & Photoresists — Dual-Source Programme, 2026–2028

*Parameter note: all lead times, cost ratios and coverage figures below are planning defaults, not measured values. Qualification durations vary by layer criticality, node, and whether the material touches a customer-qualified flow. Every number carries a re-derivation requirement against actual fab data before it is used in a capital or contract decision. Export-control status is a moving target; the jurisdictional exposure map must be refreshed monthly, not annually.*

---

## 1. The Strategic Bet

**We have been treating single-sourcing as a procurement problem. It is a capacity-allocation and incentive problem.**

Every fab in the industry knows it should dual-source photoresists and specialty gases. Almost none do it comprehensively. The reason is not ignorance and it is not supplier resistance. It is that the two things dual-sourcing actually consumes — **qualification slots** (test wafers, tool time, metrology, integration engineers) and **balance-sheet commitment** — are both owned by functions that are measured on something else. Manufacturing is measured on output; finance is measured on unit cost and fixed obligations. Resilience is a cost to both and a benefit to neither.

The bet: **treat qualification capacity as a rationed capital budget and treat supply commitment as a priced option, not a purchase.** Then move the cost of both out of the plant's cost line so the people who must spend it are not punished for spending it.

Three commitments follow:

1. **Qualification is a portfolio, not a project list.** We can run a finite number of quals per year. We will decide which ones explicitly, at board level, against exposure — rather than letting them be selected by whichever supplier crisis is loudest.
2. **A second source that is not shipping production volume is not a second source.** Dormant qualifications decay. We count only live, flowing alternates.
3. **We pay for optionality, not for inventory we do not need.** The default instrument is a capacity reservation fee against a priced downside — not take-or-pay, and not hope.

---

## 2. Diagnosis: Why Dual-Sourcing Programmes Stall

| Observed symptom | Actual root cause | Fix in this strategy |
|---|---|---|
| "We have a second source" — but it has never shipped at volume | Qualification declared complete at report sign-off, not at production flow | Liveness test (§4); minimum 10% sustained volume split |
| Qual roadmap slips every quarter | Qual competes with yield-improvement and NPI for the same test wafers; loses every time | Ring-fenced qualification slot budget, allocated by Council, not by the fab (§5) |
| Finance blocks offtake agreements | Take-or-pay lands as a fixed obligation with no matched revenue; nobody has priced the alternative | Instrument ladder + explicit option pricing against downtime VaR (§7) |
| Second source qualified — disrupted anyway | Both suppliers buy the same precursor / PAG / fluorspar from the same n-2 plant | n-2 sub-tier disclosure as an award condition (§3, §4) |
| Alternate exists but cannot be switched to | Customer-qualified flows require PCN and customer re-qual; 6–12 months of hidden lead time | Pre-approved alternate materials list negotiated at design-win (§5) |
| Stockpile "covers us for six months" | Shelf life, cold chain, and hazmat permit limits were never checked | Shelf-life- and permit-adjusted cover, buffered at the least perishable point (§8) |
| Plant resists switching volume to the alternate | Alternate carries a price premium that hits the plant's material cost variance | Resilience premium booked to a corporate assurance-of-supply line (§7) |

**Do not solve this by mandating "dual-source everything."** That spreads a fixed qualification capacity across too many materials and completes none of them. Solve it by ruthless tiering and by fixing the two resource constraints that actually bind.

---

## 3. Material Criticality Tiering

Exposure is not supplier count. Score every material on **four independent concentration dimensions** — a material can be dual-sourced on one and single-pointed on another.

| Dimension | Question | Typical blind spot |
|---|---|---|
| **Entity** | How many legal suppliers? | Two suppliers, one of which resells the other's product |
| **Site** | How many producing plants? | Two suppliers, adjacent plants on one industrial estate, one utility feed |
| **Jurisdiction** | How many export-control regimes? | Both alternates in one country; one licence decision closes both |
| **Sub-tier (n-2/n-3)** | How many sources of the key precursor, monomer, PAG, or feedstock mineral? | The real chokepoint in resists and fluorinated gases |

Then tier on **Time-to-Recover vs. Time-to-Survive**:

- **TTR** = realistic time to restore supply after loss of the primary node (includes re-permitting, re-qual, and customer PCN, not just shipping).
- **TTS** = days the fab can run on buffer + qualified alternate capacity at current loading.
- **Exposure gap = TTR − TTS.** Value at Risk = gap (days) × revenue-per-day of the wafer layers that material touches.

| Tier | Definition | Illustrative population | Governance load |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M1 — Node-critical, single-point** | Gap > 60 days; no qualified alternate; touches every wafer at a critical layer | EUV/ArF-i resist systems and their PAG/polymer chain; C₄F₆ and select etch gases; specific ALD/CVD precursors; CMP pad; high-purity HF; enriched ¹¹B species | Council-mandated dual-source programme; funded capacity reservation; monthly board metric; no node freeze without a funded alternate path |
| **M2 — Concentrated, substitutable with effort** | Gap 15–60 days; alternate technically feasible in 12–18 months | Bulk specialty gases (NF₃, WF₆, silanes, HBr); slurries; electronic-grade wet chemistries; rare gases | Dual-source target with dated plan; buffer to close gap in the interim |
| **M3 — Commodity / deep market** | Gap < 15 days; ≥3 independent qualified sources | Bulk gases, standard solvents, consumables | Standard sourcing; annual concentration recheck only |

**Tier discipline:** M1 materials may not be re-tiered downward on the basis of a supplier's assurance. Only a demonstrated, live alternate moves a material out of M1. Expect the M1 list to be **12–25 materials**, not 200. If it is longer than 30, the tiering is not doing its job and the qualification portfolio will fail.

---

## 4. The Resilience Standard — Four Testable Conditions

A material is counted as dual-sourced only if it passes all four. Failing any one, it stays on the M1 register and continues to consume management attention.

| Test | Question | Evidence required |
|---|---|---|
| **Independence** | Are the two sources independent on entity, site, jurisdiction *and* n-2? | Sub-tier map to n-2 minimum, supplier-attested, audit-right backed; distinct export-control jurisdictions for M1 |
| **Liveness** | Has the alternate shipped production volume recently? | ≥10% of trailing-6-month volume through the alternate, at production spec, on production tooling. A qual report is not evidence |
| **Depth** | Can the alternate absorb the primary's volume, and how fast? | Written surge capacity, ramp curve in weeks, and a **pre-agreed allocation ranking** in the contract's force-majeure clause |
| **Recoverability** | Is TTS ≥ TTR under a realistic loss scenario? | Shelf-life- and permit-adjusted cover calculation, plus customer PCN timeline included in TTR |

**The Liveness test is the one that will be waived under pressure** — because running 10% through a pricier alternate raises unit cost this quarter, and the qual "already passed." It should not be waived. Dormant quals decay: supplier lines age, lot-to-lot chemistry drifts, the engineers who ran the qual leave, and the first production lot after 18 months dormant behaves like a new qualification. A dormant alternate is a document, not a supply chain.

---

## 5. Qualification: Rationed Capacity, Not a Budget Line

**The binding constraint is test wafers, tool time and integration engineers — not money.** Treat qualification slots as a scarce capital allocation.

**Slot budget.** Fix an annual qualification capacity

Propose a supply-chain resilience strategy for dual-sourcing critical semiconductor materials, balancing qualification lead times, quality risk, and long-term commitment economics.
